step1_summary: Chief complaint: “Not having much of an appetite and energy lately.”  Additional concerns of low mood, episodic short-of-breath feelings with palpitations in elevators, and unintentional weight loss.

Symptoms:  • Loss of appetite x ~3.5 months; no specific food triggers.  • Fatigue/low energy over ‘months’.  • Unintentional weight loss ≈1 stone (~6 kg) over ≈6 months.  • Occasional nausea without vomiting.  • Headaches at work.  • Episodic palpitations + sensation of not getting air mainly in a lift; no chest pain; can walk a mile without dyspnoea (has been sedentary recently).  • Bowels normal: no diarrhoea, blood, mucus or pain.  • No reflux.  • Libido/nightly-activity decline reported by wife.
Past medical history: Primary hypothyroidism (previously on levothyroxine). No recent blood tests.
Medications / allergies: Stopped levothyroxine several months ago after changing doctors.  No current meds or allergies mentioned.
Family / social history: 35-y-old male lawyer. Job change ~3.5 months ago (possible stress). No smoking, alcohol or family history provided.
Vital signs / exam: Tele-visit – no vitals. No physical exam performed. Patient denies objective exertional dyspnoea and chest pain.
Labs / imaging: None to date; clinician plans routine blood panel (CBC, U&E, LFTs, vitamins, thyroid profile).

V: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia / other arrhythmia: could cause palpitations and perceived breathlessness.
Pulmonary embolism (sub-acute): weight loss and unexplained dyspnoea can occur, but lack of exertional SOB makes this less likely.
I: Chronic infection such as tuberculosis: systemic symptoms of weight loss, anorexia, fatigue.
Subacute thyroiditis (inflammatory): can give fluctuating thyroid levels → palpitations, weight/appetite change.
N: Lymphoma or other haematologic malignancy: B-symptoms include weight loss, fatigue, night sweats (not reported).
Gastro-intestinal malignancy (e.g., gastric/colonic cancer): anorexia, weight loss, nausea.
D: Major depressive disorder: classic triad of low mood, anhedonia, reduced appetite/weight loss, fatigue.
Iron-deficiency or other anaemia: fatigue, exertional intolerance, pallor, sometimes pica; could coexist with appetite issues.
Relapsed hypothyroidism from stopping levothyroxine: can cause fatigue, low mood, slowed bowels; classically weight gain but appetite may fall.
I2: Medication withdrawal (levothyroxine cessation) → hypothyroid state with fatigue, low mood.
Excess caffeine or stimulant use (work-related) → palpitations, nausea, decreased appetite.
C: No relevant congenital disorders identified from history.
A: Autoimmune Addison’s disease: weight loss, anorexia, nausea, fatigue, hypotension; often accompanies other autoimmune disease such as Hashimoto’s.
T: Psychological/physiological stress reaction or panic attacks (can be considered a ‘trauma/stress’ response) producing palpitations and breathlessness.
E: Hyperthyroidism (endocrine): palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance; could reflect thyroid over-activity after variable dosing/stopping meds.
Diabetes mellitus (metabolic): weight loss and fatigue if hyperglycaemia unchecked.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Temporal link to job change, persistent low mood, loss of appetite, weight loss, fatigue, decreased libido, and intact exercise tolerance point toward a primary mood disorder with somatic overlap.
supporting_evidence: Patient describes feeling "down", lacking energy, "nothing is feeling right".
Loss of appetite and ≈1-stone weight loss over months.
Decreased libido/"wife complaining about nightly activities".
Headaches, nausea, and palpitations can be somatic manifestations of depression/anxiety.
opposing_evidence: Patient hesitant to label self as ‘depressed’.
Still functioning at work (“I can do my work; that’s ok”).

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Relapsed / undertreated hypothyroidism due to stopping levothyroxine
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: History of primary hypothyroidism with complete cessation of replacement therapy months ago plausibly accounts for fatigue, low mood and appetite change.
supporting_evidence: Documented underactive thyroid; patient stopped thyroxine after switching doctor.
Fatigue, low mood, poor appetite consistent with hypothyroidism.
opposing_evidence: Unintentional weight loss (hypothyroid classically causes weight gain).
Episodes of palpitations more typical of hyper- rather than hypothyroidism.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Anaemia can cause fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, headaches, and sometimes pica/nausea; chronic occult blood loss or poor intake could coexist with appetite loss and weight decline.
supporting_evidence: Reduced appetite and weight loss may reflect underlying chronic illness.
opposing_evidence: Patient can walk a mile without dyspnoea; no overt pallor mentioned.
Bowels reported normal with no blood or change in pattern.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Brief episodes in elevators with palpitations and perceived inability to breathe suggest situational anxiety or panic; may coexist with depression.
supporting_evidence: Palpitations + dyspnoea described in lift; resolves outside stimulus.
Job stress and overall low mood.
No chest pain; normal exertional capacity.
opposing_evidence: Patient denies specific claustrophobia; episodes occur ‘every time’ in lift but unclear elsewhere.
Core persistent symptoms (fatigue, appetite loss) better explained by depression or medical causes.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, and nausea could represent adrenal insufficiency, especially given co-existing autoimmune thyroid disease.
supporting_evidence: Unintentional weight loss and chronic fatigue.
History of autoimmune thyroid disease (shared predisposition).
opposing_evidence: No postural dizziness, hyperpigmentation, salt craving or hypotension reported.
Palpitations situational; Addison’s usually gives hypotension rather than tachyarrhythmia.
